$$\therefore$$ Rate at which the shortest distance between $$x$$ and $$y$$ is increasing is $$\sqrt{37} \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$$.

en.content: Two radioactive materials X$$_1$$ and X$$_2$$ have decay constant 5$$\lambda$$ and $$\lambda$$, respectively. If initially they have the same number of nuclei, then the ratio of the number of nuclei of X$$_1$$ to X$$_2$$ will be $$1/e$$ after a time
en.explanation:
Decays constants of radioactive materials $$X_1$$ and $$X_2$$ is given as $$\lambda_1=5\lambda$$ and $$\lambda_2=\lambda$$

If $$N_0$$ be the initial number of nuclei in both radioactive materials, then according to radioactive decay law,

$${N_{{X_1}}} = {N_0}{e^{ - {\lambda _1}t}}$$

and $${N_{{X_2}}} = {N_0}{e^{ - {\lambda _2}t}}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${{{N_{{X_1}}}} \over {{N_{{X_2}}}}} = {{{N_0}{e^{ - {\lambda _1}t}}} \over {{N_0}{e^{ - {\lambda _2}t}}}}$$

$$\frac{1}{e}=e^{\left(-\lambda_1+\lambda_2\right) t}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & {\left[\text { Given, } \frac{N_{X_1}}{N_{X_2}}=\frac{1}{e}\right]} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad e^{-1}=e^{-\left(\lambda_1-\lambda_2\right) t} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\left(\lambda_1-\lambda_2\right) t=1 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad t=\frac{1}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5 \lambda-\lambda}=\frac{1}{4 \lambda} \\ & \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The Poisson's ratio of a material is 0.1. If the longitudinal strain of a rod of this material is $$10^{-3}$$, then the percentage change in the volume of the rod will be
en.explanation:
If $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ be the longitudinal strain and lateral strain respectively, then

$$\alpha =\frac{l_2-l_1}{l_1}=10^{-3}=0.001$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{l_2}{l_1} =1.001$$ ...... (i)

$$\text { Poisson's ratio, } \sigma=\frac{\text { Lateral strain }}{\text { Longitudinal strain }}$$

$$\begin{array}{rlrl} =\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \\ \Rightarrow & \beta=\sigma \alpha=0.1 \times 10^{-3}=10^{-4} \\ \text { But, } & \beta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{r_1} \end{array}$$

$$\frac{r_1-r_2}{r_1}=10^{-4}=0.0001$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{r_2}{r_1}=0.9999$$ ..... (ii)

Hence, percentage increase in volume

$$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{V_2-V_1}{V_1} \times 100 \\ & =\frac{\pi r_2^2 l_2-\pi r_1^2 l_1}{\pi r_1^2 l_1} \times 100 \\ & =\left[\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^2\left(\frac{l_2}{l_1}\right)^2-1\right] \times 100 \\ & =\left[(0.9999)^2 \times(1.0001)^2-1\right] \times 100 \\ & =0.0008 \times 100=0.08 \% \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A satellite can be in a geostationary orbit around a planet if it is at a distance R from the centre of the planet. If the planet starts rotating about its axis with double the angular velocity, then to make the satellite geostationary, its orbital radius should be
en.explanation:
We know that, angular velocity,

$$\omega = {{2\pi } \over T}$$

$$ \Rightarrow T = {{2\pi } \over \omega }$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{{T_2}} \over {{T_1}}} = {{{\omega _1}} \over {{\omega _2}}}$$

$$ = {{{\omega _1}} \over {2{\omega _1}}}$$ [$$\because$$ $${\omega _2} = 2{\omega _1}$$]

$$ \Rightarrow {{{T_2}} \over {{T_1}}} = {1 \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {T_2} = {{{T_1}} \over 2}$$ .... (i)

According to Kepler's law,

$$\begin{aligned} T^2 & \propto R^3 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & R\propto T^{2 / 3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{R_2}{R_1} & =\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{2 / 3} \\ & =\left(\frac{T_1 / 2}{T}\right)^{2 / 3} \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2 / 3} \\ R_2 & =\frac{R_1}{2^{2 / 3}} \\ & =\frac{R}{4^{1 / 3}} \end{aligned} $$

en.content: A frame made of metallic wire enclosing a surface area A is covered with a soap film. If the area of the frame of metallic wire is reduced by 50%, then the energy of the soap film will be changed by
en.explanation:

Final surface area, A$$_2$$ = A$$_1$$ $$-$$ 50% of A

A$$_2$$ = A $$-$$ 50% of A = $$A-\frac{A}{2}=\frac{A}{2}$$

Initial surface energy, $$E_1=T.2A=2TA$$ ..... (i)

Final surface energy, E$$_2$$ = Surface tension $$\times$$ Surface area

$$ \Rightarrow {E_2} = T \times 2({A_1} - {A_2})$$

$$ = T \times 2\left( {A - {A \over 2}} \right)$$

$$ = T \times 2 \times {A \over 2}$$

$$\Rightarrow E_2=TA$$

$$\therefore$$ Percentage change in the energy of soap film

$$ = {{{E_1} - {E_2}} \over {{E_1}}} \times 100$$

$$ = {{2TA - TA} \over {2TA}} \times 100$$

$$ = 50\% $$

en.content: A compound slab is made of two parallel plates of copper and brass of the same thickness and having thermal conductivities in the ratio 4 : 1. The free face of copper is at 0$$^\circ$$C. Rate of flow of heat will be equal in both the plates as connected in series.

$$ \Rightarrow {{\theta - 20} \over {20}} = {{{K_{copper}}} \over {{K_{brass}}}} = {4 \over 1}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \theta - 20 = 80$$

$$\theta = 100\Upsilon C$$

en.content:
In mm$$^3$$ of a gas is compressed at 1 atmospheric pressure and temperature 27$$^\circ$$C to 627$$^\circ$$C. What is the final pressure under adiabatic condition?

($$\gamma$$ for the gas = 1.5)
en.explanation:
Given,

$$\begin{aligned} V_1 & =1 \mathrm{~mm}^3 \\ & =10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}^3 \\ p_1 & =1 \mathrm{~atm} \\ & =1 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2 \\ T_1 & =27+273 \\ & =300 \mathrm{~K} \\ T_2 & =627+273 \\ & =900 \mathrm{~K} \end{aligned}$$

Under adiabatic condition,

$$\begin{aligned} p_1^{1-\gamma} T_1^\gamma & =p_2^{1-\gamma} T_2^\gamma \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)^{1-\gamma} & =\left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^\gamma \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)^{1-1.5} & =\left(\frac{300}{900}\right)^{1.5} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)^{-0.5} & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{1.5} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^{0.5} & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{1.5} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{p_1}{p_2}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\frac{1.5}{0.5}}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3=\frac{1}{27} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad p_2=27 p_1=27 \times 1 \times 10^5 \\ & =27 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2 \\ & \end{aligned}$$

en.content: If sink is at a temperature of $$-39\Upsilon$$C and source at 0$$^\circ$$C, then efficiency will be

en.content: A particle of mass m is moving in a horizontal circle of radius R under a centripetal force equal to $$-\frac{A}{R^2}$$ (A = constant). The total energy of the particle is
en.explanation:
Given, centripetal force, $$F=-\frac{A}{R^2}$$

$$\therefore$$ Potential energy, $$U=-\frac{d F}{d R}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & =-\frac{d}{d R}\left(-\frac{A}{R^2}\right) \\ & =-\frac{A}{R} \end{aligned}$$

In circular motion, centripetal force is responsible for the motion of object.

$$\begin{array} & \therefore & \frac{m v^2}{R} & =\frac{A}{R^2} \\ \Rightarrow & m v^2 & =\frac{A}{R} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{1}{2} m v^2 & =\frac{A}{2 R} \end{array}$$

$$\therefore$$ Kinetic energy, $$K=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{A}{2 R}$$

$$\therefore$$ Total energy $$=U+K$$

$$=-\frac{A}{R}+\frac{A}{2 R}=-\frac{A}{2 R} $$

en.content: A force of 20 N is applied on a body of mass 5 kg resting on a horizontal plane. The body gains a kinetic energy of 10 J after it moves a distance 2 m. The frictional force is
en.explanation:
Given, force $$F=20 \mathrm{~N}$$

$$m=5 \mathrm{~kg}$$

Net force on the body,

$$F_{\text {net }}=F-f_s$$

[where, $$f_s=$$ friction]

$$\therefore$$ Work done by displacing $$2 \mathrm{~m}$$ is given as

$$\begin{aligned}W & =F_{\text {net }} \times \text { displacement } \\ & =\left(F-f_s\right) 2 \\ & =\left(20-f_s\right) 2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad W & =40-2 f_s \end{aligned}$$

According to work-energy theorem,

Work done = gain in kinetic energy

$$\Rightarrow 40-2 f_s =10$$

$$\Rightarrow 2 f_s=40-10 =30$$

$$\Rightarrow f_s =\frac{30}{2}$$

$$=15 \mathrm{~N}$$

en.content: A body under the action of a force $$F = 6\widehat i - 8\widehat j + 10\widehat k$$, acquires an acceleration of 1 m/s2. The mass of this body must be

en.content: A body of mass 1000 kg is moving horizontally with a velocity 50 m/s. A mass of 250 kg is added. Find the final velocity.
en.explanation:
Mass of the body, $$m=1000 \mathrm{~kg}$$

$$v=50 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$$

After adding $$250 \mathrm{~kg}$$, new mass of the body,

$$\begin{aligned}m^{\prime} & =m+250 \\ & =1000+250 \\ & =1250 \mathrm{~kg} \end{aligned}$$

If $$v'$$ be the final velocity of the body, then by conservation of linear momentum,

$$\begin{aligned}m v & =m^{\prime} v^{\prime} \\ \Rightarrow 1000 \times 50 & =1250 \times v^{\prime} \\ \Rightarrow \quad v^{\prime} & =\frac{1000 \times 50}{1250} \\ & =40 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Equal volumes of two gases, having their densities in the ratio of 1 : 16 exert equal pressures on the walls of two containers. The ratio of their rms velocities $$\left(\frac{c_1}{c_2}\right)$$
en.explanation:

Since, pressure of both gases are equal.

$$\therefore p_1 =p_2$$

$$\frac{1}{3} \rho_1 c_1^2 =\frac{1}{2} \rho_2 c_2^2$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{c_1^2}{c_2^2} =\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}=\frac{16}{1}$$

$$=\left(\frac{4}{1}\right)^2$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{c_1}{c_2} =\frac{4}{1}$$

$$\Rightarrow c_1: c_2 =4: 1$$

en.content: A gaseous mixture consists of 16 g of helium and 16 g of oxygen. The ratio $$C_p/C_V$$ of the mixture is
en.explanation:
Mass of helium, $$m_1=16 \mathrm{~g}$$

Mass of oxygen, $$m_2=16 \mathrm{~g}$$

$$\therefore$$ Number of moles of He gas,

$$n_1=\frac{m_1}{4}=\frac{16}{4}=4$$

Number of moles of $$\mathrm{O}_2$$ gas,

$$n_2=\frac{m_2}{32}=\frac{16}{32}=\frac{1}{2} $$

We know that for the mixture,

$$C_V=\frac{n_1 C_{V_1}+n_2 C_{V_2}}{n_1+n_2}, \text { where } C_V=\frac{f R}{2} $$

and $$C_p=\frac{n_1 C_{p_1}+n_2 C_{p_2}}{n_1+n_2}$$, where $$C_p=\left(\frac{f}{2}+1\right) R$$

For He gas, $$f=3, n_1=4$$

For $$\mathrm{O}_2$$ gas, $$f=5, n_2=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\therefore \quad \frac{C_p}{C_V} & =\frac{n_1 C_{p_1}+n_2 C_{p_2}}{n_1 C_{V_1}+n_2 C_{V_2}} \\ & =\frac{4 \times\left(\frac{3}{2}+1\right) R+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{5}{2}+1\right) R}{4 \times \frac{3}{2} R+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{5}{2} R} \\ & =\frac{\left(4 \times \frac{5}{2} R\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{7}{2} R\right)}{\left(4 \times \frac{3}{2} R\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{5}{2} R\right)}=\frac{47}{29} \\ & =1.62 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A particle executes a linear SHM with an amplitude of 4 cm. At the mean position the velocity of the particle is 10 cm/s. What is the displacement of the particle when its speed becomes 5 cm/s?
en.explanation:

A = 4 cm

At mean position velocity,

$$v_{\max}=10$$ cm/s

$$\Rightarrow A\omega=10$$

$$ \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \omega & =\frac{10}{A} \\ & =\frac{10}{4}=2.5 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$

Again when $$v=5 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$$, then displacement, $$x=$$ ?

We know that,

$$\begin{aligned} & v=\omega \sqrt{A^2-x^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 5=2.5 \sqrt{4^2-x^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 2=\sqrt{A^2-x^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 4=A^2-x^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 4=4^2-x^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad x^2=16-4=12 \\ & \therefore \quad x=\sqrt{12}=2 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm} \\ & \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The equation of a progressive wave can be given by $$y=15\sin(660\pi t-0.02\pi x)$$ cm. The frequency of the wave is
en.explanation:

We get,

$$\begin{array} & & \frac{2 \pi}{T} =660 \pi \\ \Rightarrow & T =\frac{2 \pi}{660 \pi} \\ \Rightarrow & T =\frac{1}{330} \end{array}$$

$$\therefore$$ Frequency of the wave,

$$\begin{aligned} \nu & =\frac{1}{T} \\ & =\frac{1}{1 / 330}=330 \mathrm{~Hz} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A source of sound gives 5 beats per second, when sounded with another source of frequency 100 s$$^{-1}$$. The second harmonic of the source, together with a source of frequency 205 s$$^{-1}$$ gives 5 beats per second. What is frequency of the source?

If 5 beats are produced with frequency $$105 \mathrm{~Hz}$$, then frequency of second harmonic will be $$210 \mathrm{~Hz}$$.

i.e.

$$\begin{array}{r} 2 f=210 \\ \Rightarrow f=105 \mathrm{~Hz} \\ =105 \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \end{array}$$

en.content: If voltage $$V=(200\pm 8)V$$ and current $$I=(20\pm0.5)A$$, then the percentage error in resistance R is

en.content: A body is projected vertically upwards. The times corresponding to height $$h$$, while ascending and while descending are $$t_1$$ and $$t _2$$ , respectively. Then, the velocity of projection is ($$g$$ is acceleration due to gravity)
en.explanation:
Let u be the initial velocity of vertical projection and t be the time taken by the body to reach at height h from the ground.

$$\therefore$$ using equation, $$h = ut + {1 \over 2}a{t^2}$$

Here, $$u = u,a = - g$$

$$\therefore$$ $$h = ut - {1 \over 2}g{t^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow g{t^2} - 2ut + 2h = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$t = {{2u\, \pm \,\sqrt {4{u^2} - 4g \times 2h} } \over {2g}}$$

$$ = {{u\, \pm \,\sqrt {{u^2} - 2gh} } \over g}$$

It means t has two values, $$t_1$$ and $$t_2$$. where $$t_1$$ is time taken by the body in reaching maximum height and $$t_2$$ be the time taken by the body in reaching ground from maximum height.

$$\therefore$$ $${t_1} = {{u\, + \,\sqrt {{u^2} - 2gh} } \over g}$$

and $${t_2} = {{u\, - \,\sqrt {{u^2} - 2gh} } \over g}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${t_1} + {t_2} = {{2u} \over g}$$ or $$u = {{g({t_1} + {t_2})} \over 2}$$

en.content: A fluid is in streamline flow across a horizontal pipe of variable area of cross-section. For this which of the following statements is correct?

Therefore, when a fluid is flowing through the horizontal pipe of variable area of cross-section, then velocity is maximum at the narrowest part of the pipe and pressure is maximum at the widest part of the pipe.

en.content: Four particles each of the mass m are placed at the corners of a square of side length $$l$$. The radius of gyration of the system about an axis perpendicular to the square and passing through its centre is
en.explanation:

Moment of inertia of the systems about an axis perpendicular to the square and passing through the centre is given as

$$I = m{\left( {{l \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right)^2} + m{\left( {{l \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right)^2} + m{\left( {{l \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right)^2} + m{\left( {{l \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right)^2}$$

$$ = 4{{m{l^2}} \over 2} = 2m{l^2}$$ ..... (i)

If $$k$$ be the radius of gyration, then

$$I=4mk^2$$ ..... (ii)

$$\therefore$$ From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have

$$2ml^2=4mk^2$$

$$\Rightarrow k=\frac{l}{\sqrt2}$$

en.content: A steel wire of length 4.7 m and cross-sectional area $$3.0\times10^{-5}$$ m$$^2$$ stretches by the same amount as a copper wire of length 3.5 m and cross-sectional area of $$4.0\times10^{-5}~\mathrm{m^2}$$ under a given load. What is the ratio of Young's modulus of steel to that of copper?
en.explanation:
Given, for steel wire,

Area, $$A_1=3\times10^{-5}$$ m$$^2$$

Length, $$L_1=4.7$$ m

For copper wire,

$$A_2=4\times10^{-5}$$ m$$^2$$, $$L_2=3.5$$ m

If $$Y_1$$ and $$Y_2$$ be the Young's modulus for the material steel wire and copper wire respectively, then

$${{{Y_1}} \over {{Y_2}}} = {{{{{F_1}{L_1}} \over {{A_1}\Delta l}}} \over {{{{F_2}{L_2}} \over {{A_2}\Delta l}}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{{Y_1}} \over {{Y_2}}} = {{{L_1}{A_2}} \over {{L_2}{A_1}}}$$ [$$\because$$ $${F_1} = {F_2}$$]

$$ = {{4.7 \times 4 \times {{10}^{ - 5}}} \over {3.5 \times 3 \times {{10}^{ - 5}}}} = 1.8$$

$$ \Rightarrow {Y_1}:{Y_2} = 1.8:1$$

en.content: The masses of 200 g and 300 g are attached to the 20 cm and 70 cm marks of a light meter rod, respectively. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis passing through 50 cm mark is
en.explanation:

$$m_2=300$$ g = 0.3 kg

$${l_2} = 70 - 50 = 20$$ cm = 0.2 m

$$I = {m_1}l_1^2 + {m_2}l_2^2$$

$$ = 0.2 \times {(0.3)^2} + 0.3 \times {(0.2)^2}$$

$$ = 0.036$$ kg m$$^2$$

en.content: If $$P=Q=R=10\Omega$$ and $$S=20\Omega$$, then what resistance should be joined with S to balance the Wheatstone's network?

options.content: Join a resistance of 10$$\Omega$$ in series with S
Join a resistance of 10$$\Omega$$ in parallel with S
Join a resistance of 20$$\Omega$$ in parallel with S
Join a resistance of 20$$\Omega$$ in series with S

en.explanation:
The given Wheatstone bridge circuit is shown below.

Wheatstone is balanced only when

$$\frac{P}{Q}=\frac{R}{S}$$

Thus, the value of resistance S should be 10$$\Omega$$. But it is given to 20$$\Omega$$.

Hence, to decrease its value upto 10$$\Omega$$, suppose $$x ~\Omega$$ resistance is connected parallel to it.

$$\therefore \frac{1}{10}=\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{x}$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}=\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{20}=\frac{1}{20}$$

$$\Rightarrow x=20~\Omega$$

en.content: To the potentiometer wire of length L and 10$$\Omega$$ resistance, a battery of emf 2.5 V and a resistance R are connected in series. If a potential difference of 1 V is balanced across L/2 length, the value of R in $$\Omega$$ will be
en.explanation:
The given situation is shown below.

Resistance of potentiometer wire, $$R_P=10~\Omega$$

Emf, $$E=2.5~V$$

Total resistance, $$R'=R_P+R=(10+R)~\Omega$$

Current thruogh potentiometer wire,

$$I=\frac{E}{R_P}=\frac{2.5}{10+R}$$

Since, potential difference across length $$AL=\frac{L}{2}$$,

$$V = I\left( {{{{R_P}} \over 2}} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow 1 = {{2.5} \over {10 + R}} \times {{10} \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow 10 + R = 12.5$$

$$ \Rightarrow R = 2.5~\Omega $$

en.content: An electron moves with speed of 2 $$\times$$ 10$$^5$$ m/s along the positive x-direction in a magnetic field $$B = (\widehat i - 4\widehat j - 3\widehat k)\,T$$. The magnitude of the force (in N) experienced by the electron is
en.explanation:
Given,

$$v = 2 \times {10^5}\widehat i$$

$$B = (\widehat i - 4\widehat j - 3\widehat k)\,T$$

Charge on electron, $$q = 1.6 \times {10^{ - 19}}\,C$$

$$\therefore$$ Force, $$F = q(v \times B)$$

$$ = 1.6 \times {10^{ - 19}}[(2 \times {10^5}\widehat i) \times (\widehat i - 4\widehat j - 3\widehat k)]$$

$$ = 1.6 \times {10^{ - 19}}\left| {\matrix{ {\widehat i} & {\widehat j} & {\widehat k} \cr {2 \times {{10}^5}} & 0 & 0 \cr 1 & { - 4} & { - 3} \cr } } \right|$$

$$F = 1.6 \times {10^{ - 19}}(6 \times {10^5}\widehat j - 8 \times {10^5}\widehat k)$$

$$ = 9.6 \times {10^{ - 14}}\widehat j - 12.8 \times {10^{ - 14}}\widehat k$$

$$ \Rightarrow |F| = \sqrt {{{(9.6 \times {{10}^{ - 14}})}^2} + {{( - 12.8 \times {{10}^{ - 14}})}^2}} $$

$$ = {10^{ - 14}}\sqrt {{{(9.6)}^2} + {{(12.8)}^2}} $$

$$ = 16 \times {10^{ - 14}}\,N$$

$$ = 1.6 \times {10^{ - 13}}\,N$$

en.content: A moving coil galvanometer has 28 turns and area of coil is $$4\times 10^{-2}$$ m$$^2$$. If the magnetic field is 0.2 T, then to increase the sensitivity by 25% without changing area and field, the number of turns should be changed to
en.explanation:

en.content: A coil of wire of a certain radius has 100 turns and a self inductance of 15 mH. The self inductance of a second similar coil of 500 turns will be
en.explanation:
Given, number of turns in the first coil, $$N_1=100$$

Its self-inductance, $$L_1=15 \mathrm{mH}=1.5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{H}$$

Number of turns in the second coil,

$$\begin{array} & N_2 & =500 \\ L_2 & =\text { ? }\end{array}$$

We know that, self inductance of the coil is given by

$$L=\frac{\mu_0\pi N^2R}{2}$$

$$\Rightarrow L \propto N^2$$

$$\therefore \frac{L_2}{L_1} =\left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^2=\left(\frac{500}{100}\right)^2=25$$

$$\Rightarrow L_2 =25 L_1$$

$$=25 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-2}$$

$$=37.5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{H}$$

$$=375 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{H}=375 ~\mathrm{mH}$$

en.content: Two identical light waves, propagating in the same direction, have a phase difference $$\delta$$. After they superpose the intensity of the resulting wave will be proportional to
en.explanation:
Phase difference between the two identical waves $$=\delta$$

For identical wave,

$$a_1=a_2=a$$

After superposition, intensity of resultant wave

$$\begin{aligned} I & \propto(\text { Amplitude })^2 \\ & \propto A^2 \\ & \propto\left(a_1^2+a_2^2+2 a_1 a_2 \cos \delta\right) \\ & \propto\left(a^2+a^2+2 a^2 \cos \delta\right) \\ & \propto 2 a^2(1+\cos \delta) \\ & \propto 2 a^2 \cdot\left(2 \cos ^2 \frac{\delta}{2}\right) \\ & \propto 4 a^2 \cos ^2\left(\frac{\delta}{2}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad I & \propto \cos ^2\left(\frac{\delta}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A plastic sheet (refractive index = 1 6. ) covers one slit of a double slit arrangement for the Young’s experiment. en.explanation:

when, $$ \alpha t = {{3\lambda } \over 2}$$

en.content: A particle starts moving from point (2, 10, 1). Displacement for the particle is $$8\widehat i - 2\widehat j + \widehat k$$. The final coordinates of the particle is
en.explanation:
Position vector of starting point $$(2,10,1)$$ of particle is given as

$$\mathbf{r}_1=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+10 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$$

If final co-ordinate of the particle be $$(x, y, z)$$, then its position vector

$$\mathbf{r}_2=x \hat{\mathbf{i}}+y \hat{\mathbf{j}}+z \hat{\mathbf{k}}$$

$$\therefore$$ Displacement, $$\Delta \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1$$

$$\begin{aligned} & 8 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}=x \hat{\mathbf{i}}+y \hat{\mathbf{j}}+z \hat{\mathbf{k}}-(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+10 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}) \\ \Rightarrow \quad & 8 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}=(x-2) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(y-10) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(z-1) \hat{\mathbf{k}} \end{aligned}$$

Comparing the coefficients of $$\hat{\mathbf{i}}, \hat{\mathbf{j}}$$ and $$\hat{\mathbf{k}}$$, we get

$$\begin{aligned}\quad x-2=8, y-10 & =-2, z-1=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x=10, y & =8, z=2 \\ \therefore \text { Final co-ordinate } & =(10,8,2) \end{aligned}$$
